Changelog

Source: NEWS.md

drawn (development version)

Wrong answers, fixed

  • Reordering, subsetting or binding a weighted sample gave wrong standard errors. The sample matched its rows to the frame by position, so a sort moved each row onto another row’s stratum, cluster or systematic position. Sorting one stratified sample by y cut its standard error from 3,015 to 1,332, and head(), s[cond, ] and rbind() were estimated as if drawn. Each row now finds its frame row through the new .row column, so reordering by [, dplyr::arrange() or data.table::setorder() changes nothing, and ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() refuse a subset, a sample bound to another, or a join that repeats rows. A sample saved by drawn 0.2.0 has no .row column and is still matched by position, so it is refused once the frame columns it keeps show its rows in another order, unless a column with a different value in every frame row, such as an id, still matches them in order; as_drawn() rebuilds it with .row.
  • Editing the frame in place after drawing changed the sample’s estimates. The sample kept a reference to the frame, so a data.table setkey(), setorder() or := on it afterwards changed the standard error, interval, degrees of freedom and design effect of a sample already drawn. In one example setkey() halved a cluster sample’s standard error; in another setorder() took a certainty sample’s design effect from 1.04 to 171. draw() now stores a copy of the frame, column names included, so setnames(), setcolorder() or deleting a column with := does not reach the sample either.
  • A certainty design over a with-replacement rest was weighted anyway. draw(weights = TRUE) checked replace only on the outer design, so design_certainty() over design_simple(replace = TRUE) or design_stratified(replace = TRUE) returned duplicates weighted as distinct units, and in one example a total a third too high. It is now refused like any other with-replacement design. Drawing it without weights is still allowed. ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() refuse such a sample saved by drawn 0.2.0.
  • Renaming, recoding or dropping a design column in a sample changed its standard errors. The degrees of freedom, the jackknife, as_svydesign() and sample_summary() read strata and cluster labels from the sample’s columns, while the analytic variance read them from the frame. Dropping a cluster sample’s cluster column set the degrees of freedom to 0, which removed the interval, and made the jackknife delete rows instead of clusters, 61% low in one example. Recoding stratum labels broke the jackknife and as_svydesign(), or gave them the wrong strata. Every path now reads design columns from the copy of the frame stored with the sample, so only y and by come from the sample’s own columns, and as_svydesign() passes the clusters to survey in a .cluster column.
  • A spatial sample analysed under another sf::sf_use_s2() setting got the wrong standard error. Which rows lie inside the region was worked out again in the current session. A sample drawn under sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE), the documented workaround for a region that crosses the antimeridian, and analysed after switching back or after readRDS() in a new session got standard errors for a different region: 5.7 times too large in one example, and 0 with a zero-width interval in another. The point estimate was not affected. ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() now check that the design still gives the frame the inclusion probabilities it gave at draw time, and refuse the sample when it does not, naming sf::sf_use_s2() for a spatial design. That includes a design that now stops, such as one whose n is more than the rows inside the region under the current setting. A sample saved by drawn 0.2.0, which records no probabilities for the frame, is checked against its .prob column instead. ?design_spatial says the setting must be the same at draw time and after.
  • The jackknife and the local-mean variance treated rows taken with certainty as random. A row that is in every possible sample was deleted, or compared with its neighbours, as if it could have been left out. With the units design_weighted(method = "systematic") takes with certainty, the jackknife averaged 181 times the true variance on one frame, and variance = "auto" fell back to it when one sampled row was below certainty. design_spread(size =) with dominant sizes averaged 1,270 times the true variance. Both estimators now hold certain units fixed, and the jackknife’s finite population correction counts only the other units. Its note says how many units it held fixed. With one unit below certainty the variance is reported as missing instead.
  • A census got a nonzero jackknife or local-mean standard error. variance = "jackknife" on a sample of every row or every cluster applied no finite population correction, giving 114 for a six-cluster census in one example, and design_spread() with n equal to the frame reported a standard error of about 5% of the exact total. Both now give 0, as the analytic estimators did.
  • design_weighted() could give a certain unit a probability a rounding error below 1. Depending on the scale of the sizes, a unit whose share came to exactly 1 got 1 - 1e-16, so .prob == 1 missed it and a census reported a small standard error under a “Deville approximation” note. A share within 1e-9 of 1 is now taken with certainty at exactly 1, in design_weighted() and design_spread(size =).
  • A certainty design whose rest drew no rows reported an exact total. When a rest of random size, such as Poisson sampling with a small n, drew none of the rows below the threshold, ht_total() and ht_mean() gave a standard error of 0 and a zero-width interval although those rows went unobserved. The total is exact only when no row lies below the threshold. Otherwise the variance is now missing, with a note naming the rows rest did not reach.
  • Units taken with certainty counted as degrees of freedom. The t intervals of ht_total() and ht_mean() counted every sampled unit, including the ones design_weighted() and design_spread(size =) take with certainty, strata and design_temporal() intervals taken whole, clusters taken whole by a two-stage design that selects every cluster, and such units inside a certainty design’s rest. With eight certain units among ten, systematic PPS reported 9 degrees of freedom where the same selection built with design_certainty() had 1, and its interval covered 79%; a temporal design whose sparse days were taken whole covered 83%. Only units below certainty count now, and a stratum or interval holding none of them drops out. A sample with no unit below certainty has df = Inf, and a certainty design whose rest drew nothing has df 0.
  • as_svydesign() left units taken with certainty in survey’s Brewer stratum. For design_weighted(method = "systematic"), design_spread(size =) and a certainty design over a systematic PPS rest, survey still centred and scaled Brewer’s approximation over the certain units, which put its standard error at 23 times ht_total()’s on a frame with four dominant units. They now go to survey in a stratum of their own, taken whole, and the two standard errors agreed within 0.03% there.
  • A blank stratum or cluster value broke stratified and multistage designs. An empty string, such as a blank field read from a file, was looked up by name, which never matches it. inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and draw(weights = TRUE) stopped with “subscript out of bounds” for a stratified design or a certainty design over one. Neyman allocation read the blank stratum’s spread as 0 and, with min_per_stratum of 1 or more, gave its rows to the other strata without a word. A multistage sample got NA probabilities, weights and totals, and sample_summary() gave a blank group an NA frame count. A blank value is now a key like any other, shown as (blank) in messages and summaries.
  • Two strata could be counted as one. Several strata columns were joined into one key with a carriage return between the values, so ("x\ry", "z") and ("x", "y\rz") made one stratum of two, and the allocation, the probabilities and the variance were all worked out over the merged stratum. Two numbers that print alike, such as 0.3 and 0.1 + 0.2, were one stratum too. Keys are now built from each column’s integer codes, which cannot collide.
  • A sample estimated under another collation could get the wrong standard error. Text strata and a text order_by were sorted by the session’s collation, which differs between the C locale of a server and the en_US locale of a desktop. Where two strata tied in the largest-remainder split, the extra row went to a different stratum in each, and a stratified sample drawn in one and estimated in the other got a standard error 5 times too large in one example. A systematic sample walked on text got the wrong neighbours for the successive-difference variance, and joint_prob() gave 0 for pairs drawn together. Text is now sorted byte by byte, as in the C locale, in every session.
  • Two cluster labels that print alike were one cluster. 0.3 and 0.1 + 0.2 print the same, and the cluster variance, joint_prob() for cluster and multistage designs, and the jackknife compared cluster labels as text. A design_cluster() sample holding both got no variance, and two rows of the two clusters got the joint probability of rows in one cluster. A multistage sample got a Sen-Yates-Grundy variance built on those joint probabilities. design_multistage() also counted the two as one cluster of twice the size, so their rows got half their inclusion probability and twice their weight, which doubled their part of an estimated total. Clusters are now compared by integer codes everywhere.
  • design_multistage() refused a factor cluster column with unused levels. An unused level counted as a cluster of no rows, so inclusion_prob(), sampling_weight(), joint_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE) and plot(type = "probability") stopped with a false “no closed-form inclusion probability”. Unused levels are now ignored, as droplevels() would drop them.
  • joint_prob() gave NA for a multistage row with no cluster. With na_rm = TRUE, a row whose cluster label is missing is never drawn, so its joint probabilities are 0, as design_cluster() gives. design_multistage() gave NA, which filled the default matrix over every row with NA.
  • inclusion_prob() overstated the probabilities of design_multistage(replace = TRUE). It gave (a / A) * m / N_h, the expected number of times a row is drawn, where the probability of drawing it at least once is (a / A) * (1 - (1 - 1 / N_h)^m). In one example, 3 draws from a cluster of 4 rows gave 0.375 against 0.289. A cluster smaller than the per-cluster take was refused as capped at its own size, which it is not with replacement. draw(weights = TRUE) refuses with-replacement designs, so no estimate used these figures.
  • A Hajek mean over one primary sampling unit had a standard error of 0. A by domain with one sampled row, or with all its sampled rows in one cluster that stage one could have left out, and a Poisson sample of one row got a standard error of 0 and a zero-width interval labelled “analytic”, because the linearised residuals of a mean sum to zero inside the one unit. survey gives the same 0. ht_mean() now gives such a mean no standard error, with a note, unless every unit of the domain was taken with certainty, which makes it exact. Rows taken with certainty count as one unit, as the jackknife and as_svydesign() treat them, so a domain whose sampled rows were all certain gets no standard error either while the design could have drawn its other rows. In one systematic PPS example a domain sampled as its two certain rows got a zero-width interval, where the domain mean’s standard deviation over 1,500 draws was 3.4. ?ht_total adds that intervals for domains with few sampled rows cover less often than level says. A domain total, and the estimator = "ht" mean, keep the standard error of 0 their unbiased estimators give such a domain, with a note that says why the interval has no width.
  • A systematic sample understated the variance when interval did not divide the frame. The sample size is then random, 30 or 31 rows for 244 rows at an interval of 8, and successive differences cannot see what that adds to a total. A constant y got a standard error of 0, and a variable with a coefficient of variation of 0.02 got 0.04 of its true variance and an interval that never covered the truth. ht_total(), domain totals and ht_mean(estimator = "ht") now add a term for the random size, and the note says so. The default Hajek mean was not affected.
  • deff() measured a design against a simple random sample of the whole frame, rows it could never reach included. A total estimates over the rows with a probability above 0, so an equal-probability sample of 20 from the first 100 of 400 rows, design_reservoir(max_items = 100), reported a design effect of 0.05, “better than simple random sampling”, and a temporal window or a spatial region over part of the frame read low the same way. The simple random sample is now drawn from the rows the design can reach, as survey measures it, and that sample gets 1. A Horvitz-Thompson mean gets its total’s design effect. ?deff says so.
  • A constant y got a design effect and a Hajek standard error made of rounding error. With unequal weights, a total’s design effect came out as 1.36e+32, “worse than simple random sampling”, and the Hajek mean’s standard error as about 1e-16, with a design effect that changed from seed to seed. A Hajek mean of a y that takes one value in every sampled row, overall or in a by domain, now has a variance of exactly 0, with a note, and the design effect of a constant y is NA.
  • Rows a design drops were counted in its finite population correction. as_svydesign() gave survey the frame’s row count as the fpc of design_systematic(na_rm = TRUE), and the jackknife counted every row of the frame for design_spread() and design_weighted() with na_rm = TRUE. Both now count the rows the design can reach, and agree with the same draw from the frame without the dropped rows. The standard errors moved by under 1% in the examples checked.
  • Size measures whose total overflowed gave every row a probability of 0. Positive weights near 1e306 sum to Inf, so design_weighted() with method = "systematic" or "poisson" and design_spread(size =) gave every row a probability of 0 and drew empty samples without a word, and a certainty design over them took only the rows above its threshold. Such weights are now divided by the largest of them first. Weights with a finite total give the same probabilities, and the same rows for a seed, as before.
  • joint_prob() treated a row given twice in rows as two rows. The pair a repeated row made with itself got the joint probability of two different rows, 0.015 for a simple random sample of 30 from 240 where the row’s own probability is 0.125, and simulate = TRUE gave it 0. It now gets the row’s own probability on both paths. rows that are not whole numbers are refused, where 1.7 was read as row 1.
  • min_per_stratum broke the allocation rule between the strata it did not raise. The rows a stratum needed to reach the floor were taken back one at a time from the others, whatever their shares, so those were no longer split in proportion to size, evenly or by size * sd. Under Neyman allocation with a floor of 4, two large strata with spreads of 1 and 3 got 19 and 101 rows where the rule gives 35 and 85, and the variance of a total was 14% higher. The weights followed the rows drawn, so estimates were not biased, only less precise. A stratum is now held at its floor or its size and the rest of n re-split by the rule over the others, as for a stratum taken whole, which under Neyman allocation is the split of least variance within those bounds. When taking whole every stratum with a Neyman share leaves rows over, strata whose allocation_by does not vary share them in proportion to size, as when no stratum varies, where they were split evenly. min_per_cluster in design_multistage() is applied the same way.
  • design_temporal() with unit = "days" or "weeks" drifted off midnight after a daylight-saving change. Intervals were a fixed 86,400 or 604,800 seconds, so in a zone with clock changes every interval after the change started an hour off midnight. A Date column then put two calendar days into one interval, which shared per_interval between them: ten days of New York dates from 7 March 2024 gave nine intervals, with 10 and 11 March in one, and draw() returned nine rows. Days and weeks now step by calendar days in the design’s zone, so every interval starts at the clock time of from and lasts 23 or 25 hours across a change. Seconds, minutes and hours are still fixed durations, and ?design_temporal says so.
  • design_temporal() placed a Date whose midnight a daylight-saving change skips or repeats at the wrong instant. Where clocks jump from 00:00 to 01:00, as in Santiago, Cairo and Sao Paulo, the Date became 23:00 the day before and fell in the previous day’s or month’s interval, and the same day written as a string did not parse. Where midnight happens twice, as in the Azores, the instant depended on the rows beside it, so reversing the frame changed inclusion probabilities and totals. A frame holding 30 December 2011 in Samoa, a day the zone skipped, stopped every function with a base R error, even under na_rm = TRUE. A Date, and a string without an offset, now stands for the first instant of its day in the design’s zone: 01:00 where midnight is skipped, the first midnight where it repeats, and the start of the next day for a day the zone skipped. A string ending in Z or an offset such as +01:00 keeps the instant it names. drawn now needs lubridate 1.9.0 or later.
  • design_temporal() with unit = "months" or "years" anchored on the 29th to the 31st ran into the next month. A window from 31 January had intervals starting on 2 March, 31 March, 1 May and 31 May, and one from 29 February by years started its intervals on 1 March in the years between leap years. Months and years are now added to from itself, and a day the month lacks moves to its last day: 29 February, 31 March, 30 April, and 28 February in the years between leap years.
  • A region given as a list of parts that together cover more than half the globe selected the rest of the globe. design_spatial() unioned the parts, and under spherical geometry the union of the two halves of a band from -60 to 60 degrees of latitude came back as the two polar caps and a strip 2 degrees wide. The parts are kept separate now, and a row inside any of them is inside the region.
  • design_spread() never drew a row whose inclusion probability was below 1e-9. The pivotal walk set such probabilities to 0 before it started, while inclusion_prob() and the sample’s weights still gave them their value, so a Horvitz-Thompson total was biased by the whole of each such row’s y. Every row with a probability above 0 now takes part, however small, and only the rounding error in a pooled probability is settled to 0 or 1.
  • design_reservoir() stopped reading a list at its first NULL element. A list was read as a stream, in which NULL marks the end, so the elements after a NULL, common in lists built from JSON or with lapply(), were never sampled, and nothing said so. A list’s length is known, so draw() now picks positions in it as it does in a data frame. Every element is an item, NULL included, and the elements keep their names.
  • design_bootstrap() renamed or dropped a duplicated column name. A data frame with two columns named a came back with a and a.1, and a tibble lost the second a without a word. Both now come back as they went in, after .replicate, as with every other design.
  • plan_size() used a proportion’s finite population correction for a mean or a total. n0 / (1 + (n0 - 1) / N) fits a proportion, whose variance has the divisor N. A mean’s sd has the divisor N - 1, and the smallest size for it is n0 / (1 + n0 / N). Plans for a mean or a total were sometimes a row too large, and a margin that N - 1 rows meet was planned as a census. With sd = 40 and N = 10, a margin of 8.4 gave all 10 rows and called it a census, where 9 meet it.
  • plan_size() added a row when dividing by response gave a whole number. 21 / 0.7 is 30.000000000000004 in floating point, so 21 rows at 70% response gave 31 to draw where 30 bring back 21, and with N = 30 the plan said the frame was too small at that response rate.
  • plan_size() took an estimate from survey passed as deff for the design effect. survey::svymean(~y, des, deff = TRUE) is a number underneath, the estimated mean, so the plan was inflated by the mean of y without a word. plan_size() now refuses any object other than the result of ht_mean() or ht_total() by its class, and for a survey estimate points to survey::deff(). A number marked with I() is still taken as a number.
  • plot(type = "probability") on a frame larger than max_dots left out unreachable and take-all rows. It drew and summarised an evenly spaced subset of the rows, so rows with probability 0 or 1 between them were missing from the line, the count of unreachable rows and the range. On a 10,000-row frame with two unreachable rows, the subtitle gave a range of 0.0499 to 0.0501 and no unreachable row; with two take-all rows it gave a highest probability of 0.0883. The counts, the range and the mean now cover every row, rows taken with certainty are counted too, and above max_dots each step covers a run of rows and passes through its lowest and highest probability.
  • plot(type = "selection") on a frame larger than max_dots could show none of a systematic sample. The evenly spaced subset of rows it drew fell in step with the sampling interval, so design_systematic(interval = 5) on 10,000 rows showed 0, 667 or 1,333 of the 4,000 rows shown as selected, depending on the start, where every start selects 2,000. Each dot now stands for a run of consecutive rows and is filled when any of them is selected, and the count under the title covers the whole frame.

Refusals and clearer errors

  • as_svydesign() and sample_summary() give the same reason as ht_total() when a sample has lost its design, and all three name the steps that drop it (merge(), column selection, subset(), transform(), cbind()) and how to add fieldwork columns instead.

  • The refusal of weights = TRUE for a with-replacement design, and ?draw, gave the bias as “about 15%”. It is a factor of (n / N) / (1 - (1 - 1 / N)^n), about 5% at n = N / 10, 58% at n = N and more beyond, applied within each stratum, and both now say so and give the per-stratum Hansen-Hurwitz form.

  • ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() refuse a sample whose .prob column was removed, is not numeric, holds a value outside (0, 1], or differs from the probabilities recorded at draw time (for a sample saved by drawn 0.2.0, from the ones its design gives). A removed .prob gave a total of 0, and a missing value gave NA with a note saying the jackknife had run. The message says that adjusted weights belong in .weight.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() refuse an infinite or NaN y, with the count and the rows, instead of returning an infinite total or standard error. A variance that overflows is reported as missing, and the note no longer says the jackknife ran when it gave no figure.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() warn, with class drawn_weight_edited, when .weight is no longer 1 / .prob. They use the design probabilities in .prob, while as_svydesign() hands .weight to survey, so after a nonresponse adjustment the two gave different totals without a word. ?ht_total and ?as_svydesign say which column each uses.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() warn, with class drawn_grouped_df, when the sample is grouped with dplyr::group_by(), which they ignore, and give the by that estimates per group.

  • A by column that the sample does not have is named in the error.

  • draw(weights = TRUE) refuses a design_certainty() whose rest gives every row below the threshold a probability of 0, such as one with n = 0, because the weighted total would leave those rows out. Drawing without weights still gives the cut-off sample of the rows above the threshold.

  • An error raised by a certainty design’s rest in draw() or inclusion_prob() now says which rows rest was given, as in “In rest, applied to the 230 rows with w below 100”. rest counts only those rows, so its own message spoke of 230 rows on a frame of 240.

  • design_multistage() refuses an n smaller than n_clusters, n = 0 included, which selected clusters and then took no rows from some of them, and a min_per_cluster that n cannot cover across n_clusters, which draw() refused only later. draw() warns, with class drawn_empty_cluster, when proportional allocation gives a selected cluster no rows, and names it.

  • A multistage sample from a single cluster gets no variance, with the reason “A variance needs at least two clusters”, as a design_cluster() sample does. The note blamed an unlucky sample for a Sen-Yates-Grundy estimate that is negative on every such sample, and a constant y got an exact variance of 0. When stage one takes every cluster, as from a frame of one cluster, each cluster’s rows are the units of the analytic estimator, so totals, means, ratios and domain means inside one cluster get the variance of a simple random sample within it. The jackknife still deletes whole clusters, so a domain mean, ratio, quantile or contrast inside one cluster gets no standard error from it.

  • ht_mean(estimator = "ht") with by refuses a frame whose by columns are missing for some rows, which could be in any domain. Each domain’s total was divided by its frame rows with those left out, so a domain of 30 frame rows, 10 of them with by missing, got a mean 1.5 times too large. The Hajek mean, the default, needs no domain sizes and is unaffected.

  • An allocation, method, unit, variance, estimator, target or type outside its choices is refused with a message that names the argument, the value passed and the choices. The message from match.arg() named neither the argument nor the value. NULL gives the default, as it did. A missing cluster label is called a cluster label by inclusion_prob() as well as by draw().

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() stop with the error when something fails inside a variance estimator, such as running out of memory. Every error was read as the estimator declining, so variance = "auto" fell back to the jackknife and gave R’s message, “cannot allocate vector of size 244.1 Mb” in one example, as the reason. Only a decline, a condition of class drawn_declined, leads to the jackknife now. inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() raise that class where a design has no closed form.

  • A variance too large to represent, from values of y / .prob above about 1e154, is reported as missing with a note to rescale y, whichever estimator ran, and the note says it once.

  • variance = "jackknife" reports method = "none" when the jackknife gives no figure, as for a systematic or Poisson sample, which is what ?ht_total says. It reported "jackknife", in by tables too. Its note for strata with one unit names them, in the words the analytic estimator uses, where it read “needs two units per stratum as well” with nothing before it, so variance = "auto" gives that reason once.

  • A df below 1 is refused. It was accepted and the interval dropped without a word. When the design leaves 0 degrees of freedom, as a Poisson sample of one row does, the note says that, and print() shows it. It blamed one unit per stratum, and was not printed beside an analytic standard error.

  • inclusion_prob(), sampling_weight(), joint_prob() and plot(type = "probability") refuse a design that draw() refuses, with the same message. They answered for it: an n of 300 from 240 rows gave every row 1.25 under design_simple(), and a census of 1s under design_stratified() and the systematic and Poisson methods of design_weighted(); an n_clusters above the clusters available gave probabilities above 1; and a window shorter than one interval, or a key missing in every row under na_rm = TRUE, gave every row 0. The same holds for an n above the rows inside a spatial region, for a region with none, and for the rest of a certainty design, checked against the rows below its threshold. design_multistage() refuses an n that even its largest n_clusters clusters cannot hold, on both paths.

  • The weights of design_weighted(), and of a certainty design over it, must be numeric on every path. inclusion_prob(), joint_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE) and plot(type = "probability") took a column of TRUE as weights of 1 and stopped with a misleading message on a factor or text one, where draw() refused all three. Every message about the weights names the column, and the one for a weight of 0 or below says to drop those rows from the frame, since every design that selects in proportion to size refuses them. ?inclusion_prob and ?ht_mean said such rows get a probability of 0.

  • inclusion_prob(), sampling_weight(), joint_prob() and the successive-difference variance refuse a design_systematic() whose order_by column is not in the frame, as draw() did. A misspelt order_by gave every row a probability of 0.

  • A missing coordinate under design_spatial() is reported in the same words by draw() and inclusion_prob(), naming the two coords columns.

  • design_stratified() accepts a min_per_stratum larger than some strata when n covers it. Without replacement such a stratum is taken whole, so the floor needs only its rows: 7 rows meet a floor of 2 over strata of 1, 1, 1 and 100 rows, where 8 were asked for. The message gives the number needed and says how many strata are taken whole.

  • Neyman allocation refuses an infinite allocation_by value, as it refused a missing one. The spread of a stratum holding Inf came out as NaN and was read as none, so the stratum with the most extreme values was allocated no rows. Finite values large enough to overflow sd() split as the same values on a smaller scale do, and a stratum of small values beside them keeps its own spread.

  • The warning for a stratum allocated no rows says when Neyman allocation gave it no share because allocation_by is constant within it. It then suggests min_per_stratum = 1, since a larger n reaches such a stratum only once every other stratum is taken whole. design_stratified() with n = 0 no longer warns for every stratum.

  • design_temporal() checks its zone and bounds when it is built. tz must be a name from OlsonNames(), and from and to must each be one date-time, date or string that parses, with to after from. Without tz, a bound that names an instant (a date-time, or a string ending in Z or an offset) paired with a clock time (a date, or a string without an offset) can fall in either order depending on the zone. Such a pair is refused when the design is built if it is a day or more out of order, which no zone’s offset can undo, and otherwise when the design is used, in the zone the window is laid out in. The message names the argument and gives its value. An unknown zone gave a raw CCTZ error from every function that used the design, and an unparseable from reached inclusion_prob() as “‘to’ must be a finite number”. The message for an unparseable timestamp in a string column lists the forms that are read, and a POSIXct column in a zone R does not know is named.

  • draw(), inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot() warn, with class drawn_geodesic_edges, when an edge of a longitude/latitude region in design_spatial() passes more than 0.1 degrees (about 11 km) from the straight line between its corners on a flat map. Under spherical geometry each edge follows a great circle, so the top edge of a box from -50 to 50 degrees of longitude at latitude 30 reaches latitude 41.9, and rows that far outside the box as drawn were sampled without a word.

  • The warning about an edge across the antimeridian has class drawn_antimeridian and gives both readings, the short way across the antimeridian and the long way the longitudes span. It said the region was “much smaller than its coordinates suggest”, which is wrong for a region meant to cross the antimeridian. inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot(type = "probability") give it as well as draw(), and inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE) gives it once, not once per simulated draw. An edge from -180 to 180 still gives it, since both ends lie on one meridian and a box between them encloses nothing. An edge along a pole, where every longitude meets, no longer does, so a cap around a pole closed along it draws without a warning.

  • design_spatial() refuses a region of points or lines, which enclose no area, and names sf::st_buffer(), or sf::st_collection_extract() for a geometry collection. draw() found no row inside such a region, or only rows lying on it.

  • design_spatial() reprojects each member of a list region to crs before combining them, so members in different CRSs work. They were refused with “region must be an sf or sfc geometry, or a list of them, not list”, which blamed the type.

  • With longitude/latitude coordinates, design_spatial() refuses a latitude outside -90 to 90 or a longitude outside -180 to 360, which sf only warned about, and says the columns may be in (lat, lon) order or hold projected coordinates.

  • The refusals of inclusion_prob(), and of simulate = TRUE in inclusion_prob() and joint_prob(), for design_bootstrap(method = "block") said each row appears n_replicates * n / nrow(data) times on average. Under the moving-block bootstrap the first and last block_length - 1 rows appear less often, and the message now says so.

  • design_systematic() given more than one order_by column says how to walk by several: add a column of ranks built from them, such as order(order(data$a, data$b, method = "radix")), and give its name. ?design_systematic has an example. The message said only that order_by must name a single column.

  • deff() of a by table says that domain estimates carry no design effect, and points to the estimate without by. It said the table “must come from ht_total() or ht_mean()”, which it did, and survey’s deff() returned NULL with a warning.

  • A by column named n, variance, se, ci_lower, ci_upper or method, or total for a total and mean for a mean, columns the table of domain estimates uses for its own values, is refused by name. The table’s column overwrote it, so by = "n" gave domains labelled by their counts.

  • A by table whose columns were selected with [ or subset() prints as a plain data frame. It kept its class but lost the attributes its printout reads, and print() stopped with “argument is of length zero”.

  • ht_total() refuses a missing y with a message that gives the share of the weight the rows with y missing hold, which is about how low a total over the other rows would be, and points to ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE), by and a weighting-class adjustment through as_svydesign(). It said only how many values were missing. ht_mean() points to na_rm.

  • plan_size() refuses an N below 1, and plans at most floor(N) rows, so an estimated N such as 240.5 gives a whole n that draw() accepts. It returned n = 240.5, which draw() refused, and n = 0 for N = 0.5.

  • plan_size() refuses a margin of 1 or more for a proportion, and says to give it as a proportion, such as 0.05 for 5 percentage points. A margin of 5 planned one row.

  • plan_size() warns that it ignores sd given for a proportion and p given for a mean or a total, and when sd is missing and p is given its refusal suggests target = "proportion". Both were ignored without a word, and plan_size(margin = 0.03, p = 0.2) said only that sd was required.

  • plan_size() refuses a deff of NA with the reason deff() gives one, a pilot without a variance estimate or with one value of y, or a mean from ht_mean(na_rm = TRUE) with y missing in some rows, whose design effect, a domain’s, is not estimated. It said only that deff must be a positive number.

  • plan_size() plans a census when the size for an unbounded frame is too large for a number, and refuses it for an unbounded N with a message naming margin and level. It stopped with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”, or returned n = Inf.

  • plot() checks palette, main and sub before it draws anything. An entry of palette the plot does not use, such as acent, an entry without a name, a NULL entry, or a value that is not one colour is refused by name, and a named character vector such as c(accent = "red") is read as a list. A colour R did not know stopped the plot partway, with part of the page drawn, and a bad surface left the margins changed for the next plot. A misspelt entry was ignored, and a named vector stopped with “is.list(val) is not TRUE”. main takes one string, one expression, or a name or call such as quote(alpha). A number, which was drawn as text, is refused, so write main = "5" for main = 5. So are an empty expression(), which stopped the plot partway, and an expression of two or more parts, which were drawn over each other.

  • A message about an argument given a function, a name, an environment or a data frame names its class, as in “not a function”. A function or a name gave a warning from is.na() as well, and a data frame stopped with “the condition has length > 1”.

  • plot() refuses an argument in ... that is not a graphical parameter, such as simulate, and names it. It was passed to the panel, where base graphics dropped it with a warning.

  • plot() names y when the population is not a data frame, where it said data. plot(type = "map") names the two columns when no row has both coordinates, where base graphics stopped with “need finite ‘xlim’ values”.

  • Messages that name a class put “an” before a vowel, as in “not an integer”, where they said “not a integer”.

  • draw(), inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() refuse a seed outside the integer range, such as 2^31, and give the range. set.seed() stopped with “supplied seed is not a valid integer” after a coercion warning. A seed, count, level or df given as text reads as the string "1" in the message, where it read like the number 1. inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() check seed without simulate = TRUE too, where they ignored any value.

  • draw(), inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() given the design first and the data second say the two look swapped and how to call the function. They said only that design must come from a constructor.

  • A design with no closed-form inclusion probability points to inclusion_prob(data, design, simulate = TRUE). It said “pass simulate = TRUE” when raised by draw(weights = TRUE) and plot(), neither of which takes simulate. A design with no closed-form joint probability points to joint_prob(data, design, simulate = TRUE) as well, where most of those refusals did not mention it, except a bootstrap, whose simulation is refused.

  • A design class of your own (see ?draw_design) is refused by draw(weights = TRUE) and the exact probabilities with a message that points to inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE), where it said “No inclusion probability method for design type”. A draw method that drops columns of data is refused by the simulations, which counted it as drawing nothing.

Behaviour changes

  • draw(weights = TRUE) adds a third column, .row, after .prob and .weight. It holds the row of data each sampled row came from. A frame that already has a .row column is refused, as one with .prob or .weight is.

  • A sample drawn from a data.table takes := without the “Invalid .internal.selfref” warning. data.table joins Suggests.

  • ht_total() of an empty sample from a design of random size, which Poisson sampling or a systematic start past the last row can give, returns a total of 0 with no variance and a note, where it stopped with an error. Over repeated draws that 0 is what keeps the total unbiased, so a simulation loop no longer has to catch it. ht_mean() refuses the Hajek mean of an empty sample, which is 0 / 0, and gives 0 for estimator = "ht". An empty sample from a design that reaches no row, such as one with n = 0, is still refused, and the message says so. ?ht_total describes this.

  • Text keys are sorted byte by byte, as in the C locale, whatever the session’s locale: the order in which strata are drawn and in which they break allocation ties, the rows of by estimates and of sample_summary(), and the walk of a text order_by. Text read from a file without a declared encoding, as read.csv() and readLines() give it, is sorted by its bytes in the same way, Latin-1 read in a UTF-8 session included. An unmarked cluster label and a UTF-8 one with the same bytes are one cluster in every locale, as they are one stratum; in the C locale they were two. Factor columns keep their level order. In a locale whose collation differs from C, a seed can therefore select different rows than it did in drawn 0.2.0, and a tie can go to another stratum. ?design_stratified gives the tie rule.

  • by estimates come out in key order: numbers in sequence (1, 2, 10, not 1, 10, 2) and factors in level order, where they were sorted as text. Domains with no sampled row are still left out, as survey::svyby() leaves them out.

  • An sf data frame can be passed as data to design_stratified() and design_spread(), and an sf sample to by in ht_total() and ht_mean() and to sample_summary() of a stratified or cluster sample. All of these stopped inside base R on the geometry column. A by estimate of an sf sample is a plain data frame without the geometry.

  • When a multistage sample with one row per cluster falls back to the jackknife and more than a fifth of the clusters were selected, the note gives the factor by which the jackknife inflates the variance between clusters. When every cluster was selected, it says that variance is zero by design and points to design_stratified(). variance = "jackknife" on a multistage sample without size gives the same factor, and when every cluster was selected says that variance = "analytic" measures the variation within clusters only.

  • A by domain gets a variance when a stratum or interval with one sampled row holds none of its units, read from the by columns of the frame stored with the sample. A domain of strata or intervals taken whole is exact, with a zero-width interval even at 0 degrees of freedom. Such domains were refused with a note saying the standard error would be understated, which was false for them. A domain with units in the lonely stratum is still refused, and when the frame has no by columns the note says the frame cannot tell. A frame row whose by value is missing may belong to any domain, so a lonely stratum holding one is refused for every domain, with the same note.

  • ht_mean() decides whether y is a proportion, and so whether its interval is formed on the logit scale, from what y is rather than from the values the sample drew: a logical y, or a column of the frame whose values are all 0 or 1. A count that came out 0 or 1 in every sampled row got a logit interval, which cannot pass 1 and so never covered a mean of 1 or more; it now gets the symmetric interval. A 0/1 column added to the sample after the draw, or a numeric vector, has no frame column to read and is still taken for a proportion when every sampled value is 0 or 1, as before, now with a note saying so and that proportion = FALSE gives the symmetric interval of a count. by estimates follow the same rule.

  • A proportion estimated at exactly 0 or 1, such as no deviations in 60 sampled invoices, gets Korn and Graubard’s beta interval, with the sampled rows below certainty as its effective sample size, and a note saying so. It got a zero-width interval of 0 to 0. For 0 in 60 from a simple random sample the 95% upper bound is now 4.87%. A design that leaves 0 degrees of freedom, such as a Poisson sample of one row, gets the Clopper-Pearson interval over the sampled rows. A census, or a domain of rows taken with certainty, is still exact. A domain’s effective sample size for the beta interval is capped at its rows below certainty, so its interval is never narrower than Clopper-Pearson’s over them.

  • Estimates from ht_total() and ht_mean() hold unreachable, the number of frame rows with inclusion probability 0, and print it on a line of its own when there are any, whether or not there is a standard error. by tables carry it as an attribute and print it too. draw() warns about such rows, but a sample saved and read back, or drawn with the warning muffled, gave a total over part of the frame with no sign of the rest.

  • The printout of ht_total() and ht_mean() shows the note whenever the standard error is 0, such as the one saying every sampled row was taken with certainty.

  • sample_summary() gains N_reachable, the rows the design gives a probability above 0, and prints the sampling fraction over them. N is still every row of the frame.

  • A stratified design whose min_per_stratum raises a stratum, or a multistage design whose min_per_cluster raises a cluster, can allocate different counts than drawn 0.2.0 did, as above, and a seed then selects different rows. Designs where no floor binds allocate and draw as before.

  • design_temporal(tz = NULL), the default, lays out the window in the zone of a POSIXct time column, and in UTC only when the column has none: a Date or string column, or a POSIXct whose tzone is empty. It always used UTC, so a window of local dates over New York data ran from 19:00 to 19:00 local time. Give tz = "UTC" for the old layout. A printed design shows tz as “from the time column, else UTC” when it is not set. This and the calendar fixes above change the intervals of some designs. A sample drawn earlier whose probabilities they change is refused by ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary(), which say the design now gives different probabilities; draw it again.

  • design_temporal() reads timestamps and bounds written as "2024-03-01 14:30" or "2024-03-01 14", with a space or a T before the time. They were unparseable, so such rows stopped the draw or, under na_rm = TRUE, were dropped. A date written day or month first, such as "01/02/2024", is still refused rather than guessed.

  • design_reservoir() returns the items of a connection or generator in the order they arrived, as it returns the rows of a data frame in frame order. They came back in the order of the reservoir’s slots. The items drawn for a seed are unchanged. A list is now sampled as a data frame is, so it gives a different sample for a seed than it did. ?design_reservoir says that the streaming path and the data-frame path use different algorithms and so give different samples for one seed.

  • design_bootstrap(method = "block") with the default block_length uses floor(nrow(data)^(1/3)) when the row count is a perfect cube too. The cube root in floating point fell below the whole number, so 64 rows got runs of 3 instead of 4, and 1,000 rows runs of 9 instead of 10. Such frames get different replicates for a seed.

  • draw() with a finite design_reservoir(max_items =) pushes the line it reads past the cap back onto an open connection in text mode, so the next read starts with it. It was read and dropped.

  • The default title of plot() names the order_by of a systematic design, its n_starts when above 1, and the within of a stratified design.

  • deff() is a generic, with methods for the results of ht_total() and ht_mean(), and passes any other object to survey::deff(). Its argument is object, as in survey’s, where it was x, so deff(x = r) must become deff(r). Attached after survey, drawn’s deff() masked survey’s and refused every survey object, such as the result of survey::svymean(deff = TRUE). Either package’s deff() now answers for both, whichever is attached last.

  • by tables gain a variance column, and their n is an integer where it was a double. The printout leaves variance out, since it is the square of se.

  • The intervals of design_temporal() are named by their start, such as 2024-01-03 00:00, in the notes of ht_total() and ht_mean(), the strata as_svydesign() hands to survey and the table of sample_summary(). They were numbered, and a note listed them sorted as text: 1, 10, 2.

  • A printed estimate names its variance method as method holds it, the name the method column of a by table shows, and says when it is an approximation: “successive difference, an approximation” where it said “successive-difference approximation”. The README’s table of designs uses the same names.

  • A printed plan_size() shows a margin of 1e5 as 100,000, where it showed 1e+05. A margin that would take many digits, such as 1e-300, stays in scientific notation.

  • sample_summary() lists every stratum of the frame, one allocated no rows with 0 drawn, where it listed only the strata drawn. It gives a certainty design the groups of its rest, after a (certain) row for the rows above the threshold, where it gave none, and groups a temporal sample by interval. The rates print with three decimals, where their widths varied.

  • plan_size() plans two rows at least when the frame has two, since one row gives no standard error or interval, and its printout says so. The result’s new raised is TRUE when this applies. A margin of two standard deviations planned one row.

  • plan_size() no longer sets capped and short together. capped means that only a census meets the margin, and short that a smaller sample would if everyone responded. capped was documented as a frame that could not reach the margin however it was sampled, though a census always reaches it, and the printout now says the same.

  • A printed proportion plan shows the p it assumes, where it showed sqrt(p * (1 - p)) as sd, and the result holds p, which is NA for a mean or a total.

  • plot(type = "probability") puts frame rows on its axis and centres a plateau on each row, so the first and last rows are as wide as the others and a one-row frame is drawn. The last row had no width, so a take-all unit at the end of a frame sorted by size did not show, and frames of two to four rows had repeated tick labels. The mean’s label sits inside the panel.

  • plot(type = "selection") and plot(type = "map") of a design that samples with replacement count draws and distinct rows, as in “60 draws, 51 distinct rows of 240”, and ring each row drawn more than once.

  • plot() of a design_bootstrap() shows its first replicate and says so, whatever its output. It marked every row drawn in any replicate, which at the default 1,000 replicates is every row. plot(type = "probability") no longer points a bootstrap to the selection view.

  • plot() passes xlim, ylim, asp and the other graphical parameters in ... to the panel in place of its own settings. Each one the plot also set stopped with “formal argument matched by multiple actual arguments”, so a map could not be given asp = 1 and the probability view could not be zoomed. In type = "probability" the rules, the axis and the mean line follow the limits given.

  • plot(type = "map") of a design_spatial(), or of a design_spread() with scale = FALSE, draws both axes to the same scale, so the map shows the distances the design works with. Longitude and latitude are drawn with a degree of longitude at cos() of the middle latitude. Other columns fill the panel as before, and asp = NA gives that back for these two designs.

  • plot(type = "map") says under its title which columns of across it leaves out when there are more than two, and how many selected rows it could not place because a coordinate is missing. It used the first two columns without saying so and counted rows it did not draw among those selected. When it thins the background it keeps at most max_dots of the unselected rows and says “background thinned to 50 of 210”. Its note “50 of 240 rows shown” came with 71 rows drawn.

  • The default title of plot(), and the description of a design in messages, gives every argument that changes what the design draws when it differs from the default: replace, start, allocation_by, cost, min_per_stratum, min_per_cluster, max_items, block_length, output, batches, scale and na_rm, the coords of design_spatial(), the above, threshold and rest of design_certainty(), and the unit of design_temporal(). Several column names are wrapped in c(), so the title reads as R code. design_simple(n = 10) and design_simple(n = 10, replace = TRUE) had the same title, as did a reservoir with and without max_items, and a certainty design’s title had no arguments at all. balanced = FALSE is left out. A title or subtitle too long for the figure is drawn smaller, down to two thirds of its size, and past that is cut and ends in “…”, where it ran off the edge of the figure.

  • A printed design shows what a default left as NULL means: start is random for design_systematic(), and n is nrow(data) and the default block_length is nrow(data)^(1/3), rounded down for design_bootstrap().

  • A seed is applied with R’s default generator, set.seed(seed, kind = "Mersenne-Twister", normal.kind = "Inversion", sample.kind = "Rejection"), whatever generator the session has selected, and the session’s generator is restored with its state. A seed drew another sample after RNGkind("L'Ecuyer-CMRG") or under sample.kind = "Rounding". A session left at R’s defaults draws the same samples as before. This holds for the seed of draw(), inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and plot().

  • draw() keeps the row names of a frame that has its own, such as the car names of mtcars, on the rows drawn, made unique by make.unique() where a row is drawn more than once. They were replaced by 1, 2, and so on. Automatic row names are still numbered afresh, and a tibble has none.

  • inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE) and joint_prob(simulate = TRUE) give a warning that the draws raise once, at the end, with the number of draws that raised it. max_items below the rows of a frame and a systematic start past the last row warned once per draw, hundreds of times, and an empty stratum or cluster was not reported. These two warnings have the classes drawn_stream_truncated and drawn_empty_start, and a random systematic start past the last row is called random, where the message named start. A warning whose details change from draw to draw, such as the empty cluster or the random start it names, is shown as the first draw gave it, with the number of draws that gave one like it. When each draw gives the same few warnings of one kind, the message says how many each draw gave.

  • inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE) and joint_prob(simulate = TRUE) time the draws after the first two, which carry one-off costs such as loading a package, and a run projected to take more than 30 seconds says how long, with a progress bar in an interactive session. A run of hours, such as the default R for design_spread() on 10,000 rows, gave no sign of progress.

  • The note of a successive-difference variance says that systematic sampling has no design-unbiased variance estimator only when the walk has a step of 2 rows or more. design_systematic(n =) with n above half the rows walked, and design_stratified(within = design_systematic()) with every stratum taking more than half its rows, have a step under 2 rows, at which every pair of rows can be drawn together. The variance is the same successive-difference approximation.

New

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() take alternative = "less" for a one-sided upper bound and "greater" for a lower bound, labelled as such when printed. The open end of ci is -Inf or Inf, or 0 or 1 for a proportion. A one-sided bound is the end of a two-sided interval at 1 - 2 * (1 - level), which is how it had to be asked for before.

  • ht_mean() takes proportion, to say whether y is a proportion rather than leave it to the rule above, and ci_method = "beta" for Korn and Graubard’s interval, the one survey::svyciprop(method = "beta") gives, with its effective sample size capped at the number of sampled rows below certainty.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() take contrast, weights over the by domains such as c(a = 1, b = -1), and return the weighted sum of the domain estimates with its standard error, interval and degrees of freedom, as a drawn_contrast. The variance comes from one run of the design’s estimator, so the covariance between domains is counted, and for simple random, stratified, cluster and multistage samples the standard error equals that of survey::svycontrast() on survey::svyby(covmat = TRUE). A difference of domain means needed linearised residuals built by hand, and the survey route stopped with an error for systematic PPS samples. The interval is symmetric, for proportions too.

  • certainty_set() gives the rows of the frame that design_weighted() with method = "systematic" or "poisson", or design_spread() with size, takes with certainty, before anything is drawn. Its threshold attribute, the smallest size among them, can be passed to design_certainty() to take the same rows with the cut-off made explicit.

  • design_stratified() takes the number of rows to draw from each stratum as allocation: a named vector such as c(north = 10, south = 5, east = 5), or for several strata columns a data frame of those columns and n. n can be left out and is their sum. A stratum of the frame with no count, a count for a stratum the frame does not have and, without replacement, a count above the rows in its stratum are refused by name. inclusion_prob(), joint_prob(), the variance estimators, as_svydesign() and sample_summary() follow the counts as given.

  • design_stratified(allocation = "neyman") takes the standard deviation of each stratum as allocation_by, from a pilot or an earlier survey, in place of a frame column: a named vector, or a data frame of the strata columns and sd. The frame then needs no such column for draw(), inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() or the variance estimators. The new cost argument takes the cost of one row in each stratum in the same forms and splits n in proportion to size * sd / sqrt(cost), the split of least variance for its total cost (Cochran 1977, section 5.5). Before, the only way to get either was a made-up frame column with the wanted spread. A stratum of the frame missing from either is refused by name, and a value for a stratum the frame does not have is ignored, so the same values serve the rest of design_certainty() when every row of a stratum is above the threshold. A negative or infinite standard deviation, a cost of 0 or less, and cost without Neyman allocation are refused when the design is built.

  • allocation_table() shows, before drawing, how design_stratified(), on its own or as the rest of design_certainty(), splits n over the strata of a frame: each stratum’s size, the rows drawn from it, their inclusion probability, the standard deviation and cost a Neyman split used, and whether the stratum was held at its floor, capped at its size, taken whole or left with no rows. It comes from the same computation as draw() and inclusion_prob().

  • design_spatial(coords =) and design_spread(across =) take the name of a POINT geometry column, such as the geometry of an sf frame, and read each row’s position with sf::st_coordinates(). A geometry column with a CRS of its own is used in that CRS. plot(type = "map") places rows by it too.

  • design_spread(across =) takes Date and date-time columns, counted in days and in seconds, so a sample can be spread over time and space together. plot(type = "map") gives them date axes. Any other column that is not numeric is refused with a pointer to as.numeric().

  • design_spread() takes strata, to spread a sample within each stratum, and allocation, to split n over them by "proportional" or "equal" allocation or by a count for each stratum, as design_stratified() does. Each stratum is scaled, sized and spread on its own. ht_total() and ht_mean() add up the strata’s local mean variances, count degrees of freedom as for a stratified sample, and refuse by name a stratum with one sampled row below certainty. as_svydesign() hands the strata to survey, and allocation_table() and sample_summary() list them with the rows each keeps once na_rm drops those with a missing value. A count for a stratum that na_rm empties is refused with that reason. The help page advised spreading within strata for large frames without a way to do it, and samples drawn stratum by stratum and bound with rbind() are refused by the estimators.

  • design_bootstrap() takes method = "circular", the circular block bootstrap of Politis and Romano (1992), in which a run of rows can wrap from the last row to the first, so every row appears equally often on average. Under method = "block" the first row and the last appear only 1 / block_length as often as a row in the middle, which ?design_bootstrap now says.

  • design_bootstrap() takes output. "indices" returns the replicates as an integer matrix of row numbers with a column per replicate, and "weights" as a matrix of the number of times each replicate drew each row, which survey::svrepdesign(type = "bootstrap", combined.weights = TRUE) takes as replicate weights. Neither copies the data. The default, "rows", still returns the stacked frame, and for one seed all three hold the same replicates.

  • design_reservoir() takes batches. With batches = TRUE, a function that returns a data frame on each call is sampled by row rather than by data frame: Algorithm L runs over the rows, draw() returns n of them as one data frame, and max_items counts rows. A seed gives the same rows however the stream is cut into batches.

  • design_systematic() takes n, in place of interval, for a sample of exactly n rows. The step is the number of rows walked divided by n and need not be whole: a start u is drawn from (0, 1), each row covers n / N of a line from 0 to n, and the rows under u, u + 1, …, u + n - 1 are taken. Every row has probability n / N, joint_prob() gives each pair the exact share of starts that take both, and the successive-difference variance has no term for a random size. Before, an interval that did not divide the frame gave one of two sample sizes, and a fractional interval was refused, so 30 rows from 100 could not be asked for. interval keeps its place as the first argument, and a seed draws the same rows with it as before. A design saved by drawn 0.2.0 and read back with readRDS() gets the fields added since, so it draws and gives the probabilities it did then.

  • design_systematic() takes n_starts, for a replicated systematic sample. With n_starts = m, m different starts are drawn from 1:(m * interval) and each is walked at a step of m * interval, so every row keeps probability 1 / interval and the expected sample size is unchanged. joint_prob() gives the exact joint probabilities, and ht_total() and ht_mean() use the variance between the replicates’ totals, (1 - 1 / interval) * var(t_r) / m, which is design-unbiased, on m - 1 degrees of freedom. as_svydesign() hands the replicates to survey as clusters and gets the same standard error. One start has no unbiased variance at all, and the successive-difference approximation was the only figure on offer.

  • design_stratified() takes within = design_systematic(order_by = "x") for systematic sampling within strata. The strata are allocated as before, and each is sorted on x and walked from a start of its own at a step of N_h / n_h rows, so every row keeps probability n_h / N_h. joint_prob() gives the exact joint probabilities, ht_total() and ht_mean() add up the strata’s successive-difference variances on the degrees of freedom of a stratified sample, and as_svydesign() hands survey the strata. Other designs as within are refused, and so is design_systematic() with interval or n there, since the allocation sets each stratum’s size. design_systematic() with neither is now built for this role, and refused if drawn on its own.

  • design_weighted() takes strata and allocation, for sampling in proportion to size within strata. n is split over the strata by "proportional" or "equal" allocation over their rows, or by a count for each stratum, as design_stratified() splits it, and each stratum is then sampled by "systematic" or "poisson" on its own, with rows past certainty taken with certainty within it. "successive" is refused with strata. inclusion_prob() gives n_h * p_i within each stratum, ht_total() and ht_mean() add up Deville’s approximation over the strata for "systematic" and count degrees of freedom as for a stratified sample, a stratum with one sampled row below certainty is refused by name, and the jackknife deletes within strata. as_svydesign() hands survey the strata, with Brewer’s approximation within each, and allocation_table() and sample_summary() list them with the rows each keeps once na_rm drops those with a missing weight. A count for a stratum that na_rm empties is refused with that reason. Samples drawn stratum by stratum and bound with rbind() were the only way before, and the estimators refuse them.

  • design_multistage() takes size, a column holding each cluster’s size measure, to select clusters with probability proportional to it by systematic PPS, taking a cluster with certainty where n_clusters times its share passes 1, and then the same n / n_clusters rows from each by simple random sampling. A row’s inclusion probability is its cluster’s stage-one probability times m / N_i, so a measure equal to the cluster’s row count gives every row n / N. ht_total() and ht_mean() use Deville’s approximation over the estimated totals of the clusters below certainty plus the variance within the selected clusters, which is the exact two-stage estimator when every cluster has the same chance, and count each cluster taken with certainty as a stratum of its rows. as_svydesign() hands survey the two stages with Brewer’s approximation at the first, or one stage of clusters when a selected cluster gives one row of several. A measure that differs within a cluster, allocation = "proportional" and an n that n_clusters does not divide are refused.

  • inclusion_prob() gives design_cluster(balanced = TRUE) its exact inclusion probabilities, where it refused them as having no closed form, so plot(type = "probability") and sampling_weight() work for it too. A row of a cluster of N_i rows has (a / A) * E(m) / N_i, the take m averaged over the selections that include its cluster, worked out from the sorted cluster sizes. The help page quoted simulated values of 0.41 and 0.34 for clusters of 4 and 6 rows where the exact ones are 0.417 and 0.333.

  • draw(weights = TRUE) weights design_cluster(balanced = TRUE), and design_multistage() without size under proportional allocation, with an n that n_clusters does not divide or with a cluster smaller than the take, conditional on the clusters it selected, all of which it refused before. .prob is (a / A) * m_i / N_i for the m_i rows taken from cluster i, and the sample records the clusters selected. The total is unbiased given the selection, and so over every selection. ht_total() and ht_mean() estimate its variance with the two-stage formula at each cluster’s own take, on a - 1 degrees of freedom; as_svydesign() hands it to survey in two stages, with the same standard errors; and sample_summary() says the weights are conditional. Proportional allocation needs min_per_cluster of at least 1 for this. inclusion_prob() still refuses the multistage cases, whose exact probabilities average the chance given the clusters selected over every possible selection.

  • replicate_weights() builds replicate weights from a sample for survey::svrepdesign(), with the type, scale and rscales to pass with them. For most designs they are the jackknife of ht_total(variance = "jackknife"), deleting units within strata with each stratum’s finite population correction and holding units taken with certainty fixed; where the default of ht_total() is another estimator, such as Deville’s approximation for systematic PPS, they give the jackknife’s standard error, not the default’s. A systematic sample, alone or within strata, gets successive-difference replicates in walk order, without the pair the circular form adds between the two ends of the walk, and a replicated one gets a replicate per start; both give the standard error ht_total() gives by default. survey::as.svrepdesign() stops on the probability-proportional-to-size and Poisson designs as_svydesign() hands over, which is a limitation of survey that ?as_svydesign now states, for a systematic sample builds a jackknife that ignores the walk, and for balanced clusters and design_multistage() without size keeps a first-stage correction the jackknife of ht_total() leaves out. Poisson sampling, which the jackknife understates, is refused, and so are replicate weights that would take more than about 1 GB.

  • frame_totals() gives the population totals survey::calibrate() takes, the column totals of model.matrix(formula) over the rows of the stored frame that the design could reach, or with table = TRUE the counts survey::postStratify() and survey::rake() take. Rows outside a region or time window, past a reservoir’s max_items or dropped by na_rm are left out, and a missing value in the rows counted is refused. A name in formula that is not a column of the frame, such as cutoff in ~ I(w > cutoff), is read from where the formula was written; a term with no frame column in it, such as ~ cutoff, has no value per row and is refused. Calibrating a design from as_svydesign() needed the totals built by hand. The estimation article has an example; calibration itself stays with survey.

  • The results of ht_total() and ht_mean(), by tables and contrasts have coef(), vcov(), confint() and as.data.frame() methods, and tidy() methods for generics::tidy() and so broom::tidy(); generics joins Suggests. confint() gives the interval the estimate holds, on the design’s degrees of freedom and, for a proportion, on the logit or beta scale, and forms it again at another level. survey::SE() and survey::cv() work through these. vcov() of a by table gives NA for the covariances between domains, which are not estimated, and 0 for two domains of a stratified sample that share no stratum. Results record variable, the name of y, so estimates of several variables can be bound with rbind() of their as.data.frame(), and n_random, the sampled rows below certainty. ?ht_total describes them under “Working with the result”.

  • sample_summary() reports n_kish, Kish’s effective sample size sum(w)^2 / sum(w^2); n_certain, the sampled rows taken with certainty, with certain_by splitting them into those above a design_certainty() threshold, those a size measure put at probability 1 and those in a group the design takes whole, whichever rows a Poisson draw happened to hold; and expected_n, the sum of the inclusion probabilities, printed beside n when the sample size is random, as under Poisson sampling.

  • plot(type = "map") of a design_spatial() design draws the outline of region, with each edge of a longitude/latitude region along its great circle under spherical geometry, which is how the design decides which rows are inside.

  • as_drawn() rebuilds a weighted sample from rows read back from a CSV file, a spreadsheet or a database table, which keep the rows and lose the design. It matches each row to the frame through .row, or through id columns named in by, and works out the inclusion probabilities again from the design. Ids that are missing, repeated or not in the frame, a frame reordered since the draw, which shows in the columns the rows share with it, and a sample short of the rows drawn, such as the rows that responded, part of a cluster or a row taken with certainty, are refused. Text such as "F" or "f" read back as FALSE, a date-time read back in UTC and an infinite value are not taken for a reordered frame. add_fieldwork() joins fieldwork results keyed by an id to a sample, in the sample’s own order and keeping its design, and refuses repeated or unknown ids and columns the sample already has; a sampled row with no result gets a missing value. A sample that had been through a file could not be estimated from, and merge() dropped the design. The refusal of a sample without its design names both.

  • compact_sample() replaces the copy of the frame a weighted sample holds with the columns its design reads, plus any named in keep. Each sample holds its own copy of the whole frame, in memory and in every file it is saved to, which hands the frame, with any personal data in it, to whoever receives the file. A simple random sample of 100 from a three-column frame of a million rows saved to 28 MB, and to 8 MB compacted, most of it the frame’s inclusion probabilities. Estimates, as_svydesign() and sample_summary() are unchanged; ht_mean(estimator = "ht") with by, frame_totals(), and the standard error of a domain when a stratum has one sampled row, need their columns in keep, and say so. ?draw describes the cost.

  • ht_mean() takes na_rm. With na_rm = TRUE it estimates the mean over the sampled rows with y present, as a domain of the whole sample, with the design’s own variance estimator, and equals survey::svymean(na.rm = TRUE) on as_svydesign(), by domain too. The printed result says how many rows were left out and that they are assumed missing completely at random, and names any by domain left without a row because every sampled row of it has y missing. ?ht_total has a section on missing values and nonresponse, with the weighting-class adjustment to use when that assumption fails, and the estimation article shows the steps.

  • design_simple() and design_spread() take reserve, a number of units to list after the main sample for replacing units that fieldwork finds cannot be reached. draw() returns the main sample and then the reserves, numbered in the order they are used by a new .reserve column; the main sample is the one the design draws without reserve. For design_simple() the list is one random draw, and for design_spread() the reserves are a second spread sample from the rows the main sample left, so they cover the space evenly too. design_spread() takes reserve only without size and strata, both refuse reserve with n = 0, and design_certainty() refuses a rest with reserve. A printed simple or spread design shows a reserve line. ht_total(), ht_mean(), as_svydesign() and sample_summary() refuse the list. The new use_reserves() takes it with the units found unavailable, replaces them with the first available reserves, and returns a sample weighted at n / (N - u) over the frame without the u units found unavailable. Its estimates describe the units that can be reached, and ?use_reserves says what that assumes. Every unit nobody visited is taken as available, which the printed unreachable line of an estimate says; the estimate keeps u in unavailable. as_drawn() rebuilds a list read back from a file through its .reserve column.

  • ht_ratio() estimates the ratio of two population totals, sum(y / pi) / sum(x / pi), such as audited value per unit of book value, with a standard error from the linearised residuals (y - R x) / X_hat and the design’s own variance estimator, on the design’s degrees of freedom. With by it gives each domain’s ratio, estimated from the whole sample. For the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors it equals survey::svyratio(), and survey::svyby(..., survey::svyratio) by domain; systematic, spread and systematic PPS samples get the estimators ht_total() uses for them. A ratio needed linearised residuals built by hand, or the hand-off to survey. Its result has the coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame(), tidy() and deff() methods of the other estimates.

  • ht_total() takes ratio, the name of a frame column x, and returns the ratio estimator of the total: the ratio of y to x in the sample times the total of x over the frame rows the design can reach, read from the frame stored with the sample. It equals predict(survey::svyratio(), total =), and when y is close to proportional to x it is more precise than the Horvitz-Thompson total. A missing x in a frame row the design can reach is refused, and so is ratio with by.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() take several column names as y, and return one table with a row per variable, or per variable and domain with by, each row what a call for that variable alone gives. Its vcov() holds the covariances between the variables’ estimates, each from one more run of the design’s estimator, (V(z_a + z_b) - V(z_a) - V(z_b)) / 2, which equals vcov(survey::svytotal(~a + b)) for the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors. ht_total(s, c("y", "w")) stopped with a message that y must be a numeric column name, and the covariance of two estimates, which the standard error of their difference needs, was not available at all. A y that is none of one column name, several column names, or a numeric vector or factor as long as the sample is refused with a message that lists those forms and says what y was, and a column that is not numeric is named with its type.

  • ht_quantile() estimates medians, quartiles and other quantiles, overall or by domain, from the Hajek estimate of the distribution function. The estimate at p is the smallest sampled value whose estimated distribution function is p or more, survey::svyquantile()’s default rule. Its interval is Woodruff’s: the interval for the distribution function at the estimate, from the design’s own variance estimator, is carried back to the scale of y, and the standard error is that interval’s width over 2 t. For the designs as_svydesign() maps with identical standard errors it equals survey::svyquantile(interval.type = "mean") except in three places, and systematic, spread and systematic PPS samples get the estimators ht_total() uses for them. For a p below the share of the weight held by the smallest sampled value, survey’s rule takes the second smallest value as the estimate and ht_quantile() the smallest. A p within 1e-9 above a share of the weight, such as seq(0, 1, 0.01)[71], gives the value at that share, where survey and stats::quantile(type = 1) give the next. A quantile at the largest sampled value, where that variance is 0 whatever y does, gets no standard error, with a note, where survey gives an interval of no width. Quantiles were available only through as_svydesign(). A logical y is refused with a pointer to ht_mean(). The result has coef(), vcov(), confint(), as.data.frame() and tidy() methods, and confint() at another level forms the Woodruff interval again. vcov() of several quantiles has NA for their covariances, which are not estimated.

  • ht_total() and ht_mean() take a factor or character column as y, or a factor as long as the sample, and return the estimated count or share of each level as a table led by a level column, with a proportion’s interval for each share and the covariances between levels in vcov(), as survey::svytotal(~f) and survey::svymean(~f) give them. Such a y was refused, and shares took one call per level with an indicator such as s$f == "a", which ?ht_mean now shows.

  • ht_total(), ht_mean() and ht_ratio() take a single number as y or x and use it for every row, so ht_total(s, 1) estimates the number of frame rows the design can reach, and with by the number in each domain. A single number was refused.

  • plan_size() takes the result of ht_mean() or ht_total() on a pilot as deff and uses its design effect. It refuses a mean when target = "total" and a total for a mean or a proportion, since the two design effects differ for one sample, by a factor of 42 in one cluster sample.
