  • plan_size() takes strata, a data frame with a row per stratum holding its size N and the standard deviation sd within it, or the expected proportion p, and plans a stratified sample: the smallest n whose split by allocation ("proportional", "equal" or "neyman", with an optional cost column for Neyman) meets the margin, with at least min_per_stratum rows from each stratum, 2 by default. A min_per_stratum of 0 is refused, since without a floor a small stratum gets no rows until n is large, and the estimate leaves it out. n is split as design_stratified() splits it, rounding included, and the split is returned as allocation, which design_stratified(allocation =) draws as given. Stratification could enter a plan only through deff before.

  • deff_cluster() gives the design effect 1 + (m - 1) * icc of taking m rows from each cluster when rows of one cluster correlate at icc, to pass to plan_size(deff =) before a pilot has measured one.

  • A plan from plan_size() can be passed as n to every design that takes n, such as design_simple(n = plan), where it was refused before. plan_size() takes several values of margin, sd, p, deff and response, one per plan, and returns a data frame with a row per plan, and as.data.frame() turns a single plan into such a row.

  • plot() takes sub, a string added to the end of the line under the title. A sub given before was matched to an internal argument of the same name, and type = "map" stopped with ‘graphical parameter “bg” has the wrong length’.

  • A sample from draw(weights = TRUE) records how it was drawn in the attribute drawn_meta: the seed, the generator, the version of drawn, the time and the number of frame rows. sample_summary() returns it as drawn and prints the seed, the version and the date. A sample from as_drawn() records that it was rebuilt, and use_reserves() keeps the record of the draw.

Speed and memory

  • Stratum and by keys are built from each column’s integer codes, so their cost grows with the number of rows, however many combinations the columns’ levels could form. On 200,000 rows keyed by two columns of 3,000 values each, the key took 8 seconds where it now takes 0.2, and at 6,000 values each it ran out of memory.
  • inclusion_prob(), joint_prob() and draw(weights = TRUE) take time linear in the number of strata of a stratified design. At 40,000 strata each took about 9 seconds. inclusion_prob() and joint_prob() now take under a tenth of a second, and draw(weights = TRUE) half a second.
  • design_cluster() and design_multistage() find the rows of the selected clusters in one pass over the frame instead of one pass per cluster. Selecting 1,000 clusters from a million rows took 16 seconds and now takes 0.2. The clusters chosen for a seed are unchanged.
  • The jackknife sums each unit with rowsum(), so its time grows with the number of rows rather than with rows times units. 20,000 rows took 2.6 seconds and now take 0.03.
  • The analytic variance of simple random, reservoir, spatial, stratified, temporal and equal-take multistage samples, alone or as the rest of design_certainty(), is computed from the variance within each stratum, interval or cluster, and for a multistage sample the variance between the estimated cluster totals, in time and memory that grow with the number of sampled rows. The Sen-Yates-Grundy sum over every pair of sampled rows, which gives the same figures, held several matrices with a row and a column per sampled row: a stratified sample of 4,000 rows took 4.8 seconds and 1.4 GB, growing with the square of the sample, and every by domain built them again. The same sample now takes 0.01 seconds, and 10,000 rows take 0.04. A census of one row gets its variance of 0 this way rather than from the jackknife.
  • joint_prob() refuses a matrix that would need more than about 1 GB, from about 11,200 rows, and gives the size and rows = s$.row as the way to ask for the rows of a sample s. It used to go on and could exhaust memory. The full matrix is still the default. Stratified, temporal, cluster, multistage and systematic joint probabilities are filled one group at a time and need little memory beyond the matrix itself, where they needed 4 to 12 times its size: a stratified matrix over 5,000 rows took 2.4 GB and 6.7 seconds, and now takes 0.2 GB and 0.4 seconds.
  • by estimates work out the strata, clusters, systematic order, certainty split, spread neighbours and joint probabilities once per call rather than once per domain, and the analytic variances of simple random, reservoir, spatial, stratified and temporal samples, alone or as the rest of design_certainty(), come from one pass over all the domains. 200 domains of a stratified sample of 1,000 from 100,000 rows took about 50 seconds and now take 0.1; 200 domains of a spread sample of 1,000 from 20,000 rows took 16 seconds and now take 0.3. variance = "jackknife" places the frame’s rows in its strata once per call too: 200 domains of a stratified sample of 300 from a million rows took 21 seconds and now take 1.2. The standard errors agree with the old ones to rounding error.
  • inclusion_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE) and the estimators of a design_temporal() sample count the rows of every interval in one pass, where they went over the rows once per interval. 200,000 rows in hourly intervals over a year took about 6 seconds and now take 0.03.
  • design_bootstrap() subsets the data once for all replicates, where it subset it once per replicate and bound the pieces with rbind(). The default 1,000 replicates of a 5,000-row frame with four columns took 13 seconds and now take 0.4, with the same rows for a seed. It warns, with class drawn_bootstrap_size, when the stacked frame would pass 10 million rows, and points to output.
  • design_reservoir() on a connection or generator grows its reservoir as the stream fills it. It set aside all n slots before reading, so n = 5e7 took 400 MB for a stream of five items. It counts the items read in a double, so a stream of more than 2,147,483,647 items no longer stops with “missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed”.
  • design_reservoir() reads a connection 10,000 lines at a time and works out Algorithm L’s swaps within each block, where it called readLines() once per line. Drawing n = 100 from 500,000 lines took 1.2 seconds and now takes 0.1, with the same sample for a seed. A larger n gains less, because it makes more swaps and each costs what it did; n = 20000 went from 2.0 seconds to 0.8.

Handing off to survey

  • as_svydesign() hands survey a copy of the sample, so an in-place sort of the sample afterwards no longer changes the survey design’s standard errors.
  • Units taken with certainty go to survey as one primary sampling unit per stratum with an fpc of 1, through a new .psu id column, so survey::degf() gives the same degrees of freedom as ht_total() for certainty designs, strata and intervals taken whole, PPS samples with certain units, and the clusters design_multistage() and design_cluster(balanced = TRUE) take whole when they select every cluster, and survey::svyciprop() gives the same interval as ht_mean(). survey had counted each certain row as a unit, and each cluster taken whole as one more.
  • A census, a sample whose every .prob is 1, goes to survey as ids = ~1 with fpc the number of rows. Under systematic PPS, alone or as a certainty design’s rest, Poisson sampling and design_spread(size =) it stopped svydesign() with “subscript out of bounds”. An empty sample is refused with a message instead of failing inside survey, and so is a certainty sample whose rest drew none of the rows below the threshold, which survey would have reported as exact.
  • ?as_svydesign, the estimation article and cran-comments.md no longer say that survey agrees with systematic PPS within 0.2%. In simulations on frames of 100 to 300 rows with gamma and lognormal sizes, standard errors of totals agreed within 0.5% in most samples and within 3% in all; those of means differed more as the sampling fraction grew, typically by 3 to 7% at one half and by up to 12%. Where the probabilities below certainty spread from 0.05 to 0.95, totals differed by up to 9% and means by up to 17%.
  • as_svydesign() labels strata built from several columns as a . b. The labels held a carriage return, which broke a CSV export of the design variables. Where two labels would read alike, the strata are numbered instead, so survey cannot merge them.
  • as_svydesign() numbers the clusters in .cluster. survey made a factor of the labels, which merged two that print alike, such as 0.3 and 0.1 + 0.2, into one primary sampling unit. The cluster column’s name went into the ids formula as it stood, so a name with a space, such as cluster id, stopped svydesign() with a parse error, and cl-1 beside a column cl was read as cl - 1, which clustered on cl.
  • as_svydesign() hands over design_certainty() over a cluster, multistage, Poisson or replicated systematic rest, which it refused as having no single survey design. The certainty rows go to survey as one more primary sampling unit beside the clusters or replicates, taken whole at both stages of a two-stage rest, and a Poisson rest becomes survey::poisson_sampling() built from the whole sample’s .prob, with the certainty rows at probability 1. Totals, standard errors, domain estimates and degrees of freedom agree with ht_total() as they do for rest on its own.
  • A sample from design_multistage(), with or without size, or design_cluster(balanced = TRUE) with one sampled row from a selected cluster of several goes to survey as one stage of clusters with no fpc. That is the ultimate-cluster design behind the jackknife ht_total() falls back to, so the standard errors agree. In two stages, survey stopped with “has only one PSU at stage 2”.
  • as_svydesign() refuses a sample with a column named .stratum, .cluster, .psu, .fpc, .fpc2 or .unit. It wrote the design into those columns over the user’s, so an analysis of such a column in survey read the design’s values.
  • as_svydesign() refuses unnamed arguments in .... It dropped them, so as_svydesign(s, ~cl) handed survey the mapped design and ignored ~cl.
  • ?as_svydesign and cran-comments.md said survey’s standard error is larger than ht_total()’s for design_spread(). It is larger when y varies smoothly over the coordinates, and smaller in most samples when y has no spatial pattern or the sampling fraction is large, because the local mean approximation has no finite population correction. ?as_svydesign also says that the agreement it states holds under survey’s default options(survey.ultimate.cluster = FALSE).

Documentation and site

  • ?ht_total said the exact multistage estimator understates by about a third with one row per cluster. It understates by f1 times the within-cluster component, where f1 is the share of clusters selected, and the jackknife used in its place overstates by f1 times the between-cluster component, which came to 3.3 times the true variance in one example with 30 of 40 clusters selected. ?design_multistage and ?inclusion_prob give the probability under replace = TRUE.
  • ?designs and ?design_stratified name all three allocation rules, "neyman" included, where they described "proportional" and "equal" only.
  • ?design_spread gives the local-mean variance estimator’s ratio to the true variance by sample size and sampling fraction, from 1.0 to 4.9 in its table and 18.9 for 4 rows from 8, and says deff() carries the same overstatement. It said 1 to 1.6 times. A ratio slightly below 1 occurs too.
  • ?design_spatial explains how the edges of a longitude/latitude region bow under spherical geometry, how to keep them on their straight lines in degrees, and how to pass a region larger than a hemisphere as a list of parts.
  • ?design_bootstrap and the choosing-a-design article say that resampling rows suits independent rows, and point a sample drawn with strata or clusters to survey::as.svrepdesign(), which resamples clusters within strata. The help page said the bootstrap was the tool for any statistic the estimators do not cover, and the article that it estimates the sampling distribution of whatever you like. ?design_bootstrap also says that n = 0 gives a frame with no rows that keeps its .replicate column, and the README’s table of designs lists the circular block bootstrap.
  • ?design_reservoir says that each line of a connection is an item, a CSV header included, and shows how to read the header off an open connection before drawing. It said that items past max_items were never read; one is read, to tell a longer stream from one of exactly max_items, and a function is called once past the cap. A connection that is not open is opened, read and closed, as read.csv() does. Under batches = TRUE only the column names of each batch are compared, and a column whose type differs between batches takes the type rbind() gives the sampled rows.
  • ?design_systematic, ?inclusion_prob and ?joint_prob say that a fixed start makes the design deterministic, so inclusion_prob(), sampling_weight(), joint_prob(), draw(weights = TRUE) and the estimators refuse it, while inclusion_prob(simulate = TRUE) reports its probabilities of 0 and 1. The table in ?inclusion_prob gave 1 / interval for every row without saying the start must be random. joint_prob() and the estimators now refuse a fixed start with the same message as inclusion_prob(), which says to leave start as NULL.
  • ?plan_size says which design effect to pass: that of ht_mean() for a mean or a proportion and that of ht_total() for a total. A mean’s design effect used for a total planned a sample that met its margin in 23% of samples, against the 95% planned. It also says that a design effect from one pilot is noisy and worth rounding up, and when deff() gives NA.
  • ?plan_size says that margin is the half-width the plan expects, so the interval a sample reports is wider about half the time, and gives the t quantile for 3, 4 and 6 clusters as 2.2, 1.6 and 1.3 times z, where it said “slightly wider”. It says that the logit interval ht_mean() reports for a proportion is asymmetric, with an upper arm that exceeds margin in most samples when p is small, and cites chapter 4 of Cochran (1977) for both corrections.
  • ?draw and ?designs say that a seed restores the caller’s random number stream and that seed = NULL draws from and advances it. ?designs said the stream was always restored.
  • ?draw_design gives the contract for a design class of your own: a method takes design and data and returns rows of data, which is enough for draw() and simulate = TRUE but not for weights = TRUE or the estimators. The site lists it under “Extending”, where it was a page with no contract beside draw().
  • ?inclusion_prob says what a simulation costs: R draws, each of which takes time in proportion to N^2 for design_spread().
  • Claims that went further than the code or the simulations are corrected. ?ht_total said the successive-difference variance of a systematic sample stayed near the truth. Its average over the starts depends on the frame, 1.6 times the true variance on the estimation article’s example; a cycle whose period divides the interval understates it as a matching period does; a period of twice the interval overstated it 29-fold in one simulation; and under a pure trend it falls towards 6 / n of the truth. ?ht_total also says that intervals cover less often than level when y / pi is skewed and the sample small, 87% to 91% in most of the cases it cites, that the Hajek mean covers less often still when y is close to proportional to size, through its ratio bias and a variance estimate that runs low, and that variance = "jackknife" declines for systematic and Poisson samples, where it said the jackknife always resamples. ?ht_mean says the Hajek and Horvitz-Thompson means coincide for an equal-probability design that can reach every row of the frame, which a region or max_items can prevent. ?designs says that only method = "successive" of design_weighted() returns rows in draw order. ?design_weighted says that Poisson sampling takes rows past certainty with certainty and rescales the rest, as systematic PPS does, where it said they were capped at 1, and puts successive sampling of weights 1:10 at n = 5 up to about 36% from proportional, by exact enumeration, where it said 35%. ?design_systematic says that start counts along the walk, sorted by order_by when given, and ?draw that a seed is sure to draw the same rows only from a frame in the same row order. The estimation article checks five designs against their exact variance at 1,000 draws, where the ratios of 0.85 and 0.87 it printed for cluster and Poisson samples were Monte Carlo error. The spatial-sampling article shows the mean it promised, and the choosing-a-design article says why one cluster sample’s design effect came out below 1.
  • ?drawn and the package description give Deville’s (1999) approximation as the variance for systematic probability-proportional-to-size samples, where they gave it for every probability-proportional-to-size design. Poisson samples get the exact Horvitz-Thompson variance. They cite Grafström, Lundström and Schelin (2012) by its DOI. The README’s table of designs gives the size of a design_certainty() sample as the rows above the threshold plus rest’s, where it said rest’s own.
  • ?joint_prob, ?design_systematic, ?ht_total, ?as_svydesign, ?design_stratified and the estimation article say that a systematic sample has no design-unbiased variance estimator at a step of 2 rows or more, where neighbouring rows are never drawn together. With n above half the rows walked, every pair of rows has a positive joint probability. ?design_stratified gave two rows of a stratum less than a step apart a joint probability of 0; that holds for rows at most N_h / n_h - 1 apart, and at a step of 3.33 rows two rows 3 apart are drawn together one time in five. ?design_systematic says that as_svydesign() refuses a replicated sample with a replicate that drew no rows. The estimation article’s sections on systematic samples no longer use one letter for both a row and the interval, and the README’s table of designs gives the successive-difference variance of design_stratified(within =).

drawn 0.2.0

An adversarial review of 0.1.0 found estimates that were wrong without saying so. Every fix below was reproduced by simulation first, and each now has a test that fails on the old behaviour.

Wrong answers, fixed

  • One sampled row per stratum reported a variance of 0. Sen-Yates-Grundy has no within-stratum pair to sum over, so a stratified sample with one row in every stratum printed a standard error of exactly zero and a zero-width interval. ht_total() and ht_mean() now decline with the reason, as survey does by default, for strata and for design_temporal() intervals.
  • A stratum allocated no rows silently biased the total. Proportional allocation gives nothing to a stratum smaller than about N / n, and Neyman allocation gives nothing to one whose auxiliary variable is constant. Its rows then have probability 0 and drop out of every estimate; one example was 84% low. draw() now warns, naming the strata and the fix. The documentation previously claimed min_per_stratum = 0 “leaves allocation unbiased” and that a floor biases a total; both were wrong, and are corrected.
  • The jackknife ignored strata. It deleted rows across the whole sample, counting the differences between strata as sampling variance: sixty times too large on a well-stratified frame. It is now the stratified (JKn) jackknife, and equals the analytic figure exactly for design_stratified() and design_temporal().
  • One row per cluster understated a multistage variance by ~30%. The exact two-stage estimator cannot see within-cluster variation when only one row is taken per cluster. It now declines, and variance = "auto" falls back to the delete-a-cluster (ultimate-cluster) jackknife.
  • Neyman allocation abandoned its own rule when a stratum was capped. The surplus from a stratum too small for its share was dealt out round-robin; it is now re-split in proportion to size * sd, as in Cochran (1977, 5.9).
  • ht_mean(estimator = "ht") printed itself as a Hajek mean.
  • design_systematic(order_by = ) returned rows in sorted order, breaking the documented promise that rows come back in frame order.
  • The documentation for design_weighted(method = "systematic") said some pairs of rows can never be drawn together and pointed to sampling::UPsystematicpi2() for joint probabilities. The rows are shuffled before the walk, so every pair can co-occur and that function answers a different design.

Variance estimators from the literature

Every estimate now reports which estimator produced its variance in method, and names any approximation when it prints.

  • Confidence intervals use t on the design’s degrees of freedom — primary sampling units minus strata (Korn and Graubard 1999), matching survey::degf(). At four clusters the normal interval covered about 87%; the t interval restores nominal coverage. df = Inf gives the normal interval.
  • Systematic PPS uses Deville’s (1999) approximation, which needs only first-order probabilities and scales each row by its own 1 - pi. It equals sampling::varest() exactly and tracks the empirical variance at 0.98, where the previous jackknife ran at 0.89.
  • Systematic samples get the successive-difference approximation (Wolter
    1. rather than no variance at all. On a frame sorted by something related to y it stays near the truth where the simple random formula overstates two- to thirtyfold. Its limits — a cycle matching the interval, or a trend so smooth the random start is the only variation — are documented.

New

  • design_spread() draws a spatially balanced sample by the local pivotal method (Grafström, Lundström and Schelin 2012): exact first-order inclusion probabilities, equal or proportional to size, with neighbours competing so the sample covers the space evenly. On a smooth surface its variance was 14–25% of a simple random sample’s. It spreads across any numeric columns, so it also balances a sample on covariates without choosing strata. ht_total() uses the local mean variance estimator (Stevens and Olsen 2003) for it.
  • ht_total() and ht_mean() take by = for domain estimates computed from the whole sample rather than a subset of it. Standard errors match survey::svyby() exactly.
  • ht_mean() accepts a logical y, so a proportion is one call.
  • plot(design, data, type = "map") places every row by two columns and fills in the selected ones — the view that shows whether a sample covers the ground.
  • Key functions carry @references to the methods they implement.

Handing off to survey

  • Multistage designs are expressed as two stages, so survey’s standard error now matches ht_total() exactly; it previously differed by up to 5–10%.
  • Systematic PPS, alone or as a certainty design’s rest, maps to pps = "brewer" and agrees with ht_total() within 0.2%.
  • A reservoir capped by max_items uses the rows the stream reached as its population, not the whole frame.

Documentation and site

  • The README is generated from README.Rmd, so every output shown is real.
  • New articles: a getting-started walkthrough, how the estimates work (every estimator, its reference and its simulation check), an audit-sampling walkthrough, and a spatially balanced field survey.
  • graphics and utils are declared in Imports.

drawn 0.1.0

First release.

Designs are objects

Sampling is expressed as a design you build and then apply, rather than a function call with the design buried in its arguments:

plan <- design_stratified(strata = "site", n = 500)
draw(data, plan, seed = 1)

A design can be printed, stored, reused across data sets, and — the part that matters for estimation — asked what it does before you draw anything.

Eleven designs ship: design_simple(), design_stratified(), design_systematic(), design_cluster(), design_multistage(), design_weighted(), design_certainty(), design_reservoir(), design_bootstrap(), design_temporal() and design_spatial().

design_certainty() composes: rows at or above a threshold are all taken, and any other design is applied to what remains. That is the standard shape of an audit sample, and the cheapest way to cut variance when a few units dominate a total. Certainty rows have inclusion probability exactly 1, so they contribute their own value with a weight of 1 and add nothing to the variance; inclusion and joint probabilities compose exactly across the two parts.

One contract across all of them

  • n is always the total number of rows drawn, never a per-group figure. design_temporal() uses per_interval precisely because that one is per group.
  • allocation always says how a total is split across groups.
  • na_rm always decides whether missing keys are dropped or raise an error, and means the same thing whether you are drawing or asking for probabilities.
  • replace always rules out weights = TRUE: an inclusion probability describes distinct units, and a sample holding duplicates cannot be weighted by one.
  • draw() restores the caller’s random number stream before returning, so sampling inside a simulation does not shift the simulation’s own draws.
  • What comes back has the same class and the same columns, in the same order, as what went in — tibble in, tibble out, with or without weights. Rows come back in frame order except where draw order is meaningful: design_simple() and design_weighted() return draw order, and design_bootstrap() returns replicates behind a leading .replicate column.

Inclusion probabilities and estimation

inclusion_prob() gives the first-order inclusion probability of every population row under a design, without drawing anything — a quick way to check a plan before committing to it. draw(weights = TRUE) attaches those probabilities and the corresponding design weights to a sample as .prob and .weight.

joint_prob() gives second-order probabilities, and ht_total() and ht_mean() use them to return an estimate with a standard error and confidence interval:

s <- draw(pop, design_stratified("site", n = 40), seed = 1, weights = TRUE)
ht_total(s, "spend")
ht_mean(s, "spend")

ht_mean() defaults to the Hajek estimator, sum(y/pi) / sum(1/pi), which divides by the estimated population size rather than the known one; estimator = "ht" divides by the true N. The two coincide exactly whenever the weights of the drawn rows sum to N — every fixed-size equal-probability design, and every stratified design without replacement — and part company when the sample size is random or the weights vary within a fixed-size sample. Hajek is usually the steadier of the two, which is why it is the default; ?ht_mean sets out when it is not, and why "ht" is unbiased only where every row is reachable.

deff() reports the design effect on either result — the design’s variance against simple random sampling of the same size, which reads as an exchange rate on sample size. Stratifying on a variable that matters can put it far below 1; clustering on the same variable puts it well above.

The variance estimator matches how each design randomises: Sen-Yates-Grundy for fixed-size designs, the independent-units form for Poisson sampling, the cluster-level form for cluster designs — whose row count is random whenever clusters differ in size — and, for a certainty design, whatever rest uses, since certainty rows are in every possible sample and contribute nothing.

Where a design has inclusion probabilities but no closed-form joint ones, ht_total() falls back to a delete-a-group jackknife and reports which method it used, or "none" where neither could produce a figure. The jackknife is declined for systematic sampling, which has a single primary sampling unit, and for Poisson sampling, which has an exact variance already.

Every analytic estimator is checked in the test suite against the empirical sampling variance of its own estimator, every inclusion and joint probability against the observed frequency over thousands of draws, and every design that survey can express against survey::svytotal().

Planning a sample, and checking one

plan_size() solves for n given the precision wanted, rather than asking for a guess. It takes a margin of error and a measure of spread, and applies three corrections: a finite population correction from N, an inflation for the design from deff, and an inflation for non-response from response. It works for a mean, a proportion or a total, and says so plainly when the margin asked for is unreachable by sampling.

plan_size(margin = 5, sd = 40, N = 20000, deff = 2.5, response = 0.7)

sample_summary() reports what was drawn against what was there: the sampling fraction, the range and coefficient of variation of the design weights, the per-stratum or per-cluster counts against the frame, and the number of rows the design could never have reached.

Handing off to the survey package

as_svydesign() builds a survey::svydesign() object from a drawn sample, so the analysis this package does not do — subpopulation estimates, regression, calibration, quantiles with proper standard errors — can be done by the package that does.

The two packages compute variance from different starting points: this one from the design’s joint inclusion probabilities, survey from the design’s shape. Each design is therefore expressed in survey’s own terms — strata for a stratified or temporal design, cluster ids for a cluster design, survey::poisson_sampling() for Poisson, and a taken-whole stratum for the certainty rows. Totals and standard errors then agree to floating point for every design but two: survey uses the ultimate-cluster approximation for multistage designs, and returns the conservative simple-random figure for systematic sampling where ht_total() declines to return one. ?as_svydesign has the table. Compositions with no single survey equivalent — a certainty design over a cluster, multistage or Poisson rest — are refused rather than approximated.

Seeing a design

plot(design, data) shows which rows a design selects — every frame row as a dot, selected ones filled in — and type = "probability" plots inclusion probability against frame position. Base graphics, no plotting dependency.

Allocation

design_stratified() accepts allocation = "neyman" with allocation_by, giving strata shares proportional to size * sd. That minimises the variance of a total for a fixed n by putting more rows where the values vary most.

Saying when it cannot

Not every design has a closed-form inclusion probability, and the ones that don’t report that rather than returning an approximation:

  • design_cluster(balanced = TRUE) — the per-cluster take is the smallest selected cluster’s size, which is random.
  • design_multistage(allocation = "proportional") — the second-stage allocation depends on which clusters were selected.
  • design_multistage() where the per-cluster take is not constant — n not divisible by n_clusters, or a cluster smaller than n / n_clusters. The allocation runs over the selected clusters, so a row’s probability depends on which others were drawn.
  • design_weighted(method = "successive") — successive sampling has no closed form. This is the default, and the reason the other two methods exist.
  • design_bootstrap() — resampling a sample is not a probability sample of a finite population.

simulate = TRUE estimates any of them by Monte Carlo, for first-order probabilities and, in joint_prob(), for second-order ones — which is the general answer where no formula exists, including design_weighted(method = "systematic"), whose joint probabilities depend on the order units are visited. design_bootstrap() is the one exception, and simulating it is refused: every row appears in some replicate, so the count converges to 1 for all of them. Systematic sampling has first-order probabilities but no design-unbiased variance at all, because most pairs of rows can never co-occur; ht_total() says so instead of returning a number.

Probability proportional to size

design_weighted() offers three methods, and they are not interchangeable:

method Inclusion probabilities Sample size
"successive" (default) Not proportional to weight, no closed form Fixed
"systematic" Exactly n * p_i Fixed
"poisson" Exactly n * p_i Random, mean n

The default is what base::sample(prob = ) does: a good way to bias selection toward heavy units, but the weights govern each sequential draw rather than the probability of ending up in the sample. Use "systematic" or "poisson" when the sample will be estimated from. Units heavy enough that n * p_i > 1 are taken with certainty and the remainder rescaled, iterating until every probability is valid.

Notes

  • sf is a suggested dependency, needed only by design_spatial(), and survey only by as_svydesign(). Nothing else requires either.
  • Under spherical geometry a longitude/latitude polygon whose edge spans more than 180 degrees is drawn the short way across the antimeridian, so a “whole world” rectangle collapses to a narrow strip. design_spatial() warns when a region has such an edge.
  • Reservoir sampling takes a vectorised path for a data frame, whose length is already known, and Algorithm L for a genuine stream — a connection or a generator function.
  • Calendar units in design_temporal() step by calendar months and years, not by fixed 30.44-day durations.
